canonical_statement: The study asked whether a lightweight multimodal pre-flight estimator can predict frontier-LLM performance across reasoning budgets before inference and thereby support compute-optimal document inference.

BudgetDoc was built from 360 unique base document-prompt contexts across RVL-CDIP, TAT-QA, and CheckboxQA, exhaustively evaluated across five frontier models and five reasoning-budget classes to yield 9,000 labeled configuration-outcome pairs.

BudgetDoc was split at the unique base-document level into 240 training documents (6,000 pairs), 20 validation documents (500 pairs), and 100 held-out test documents (2,500 pairs) to prevent row-level leakage across configurations of the same document.
Per-configuration F1 scores were discretized into seven ordinal performance classes from Class 0 (F1 < 0.5) through Class 6 (F1 >= 0.99).

DRB combines a SigLIP-2-Large-patch16-512 visual encoder, a Qwen3-0.6B prompt encoder, learned model and budget embeddings, a 12-layer cross-page fusion transformer, and a 2048-unit MLP classification head.
DRB was trained for 20 epochs on an NVIDIA A100 80GB with AdamW, learning rate 5e-5, and batch size 4.

At inference, hierarchical scanning evaluates budget levels from lowest to highest, stops early when DRB predicts Class 6, and otherwise selects the budget with the highest predicted performance class using lower cost as a tie-breaker.

Single-model experiments compared DRB-guided allocation with the same target model run at its maximum reasoning budget; the exploratory model-selection case study used the best single model at maximum or auto budget as an oracle baseline.
The primary quality metric was F1; the study also reported API cost per sample and latency, and adjusted DRB cost included estimator compute overhead based on empirical scanning latency.

Adjusted DRB system cost was defined as reasoning-budget API cost plus empirical mean scanning latency multiplied by $0.00015 per second, corresponding to the stated $0.54/hour GCP T4 deployment cost.
On the 2,500-pair BudgetDoc test set, DRB achieved a weighted F1 of 0.753 for seven-class performance estimation.
For BudgetDoc Class 6 (F1 >= 0.99), DRB recall was 0.932.
For BudgetDoc Class 6 (F1 >= 0.99), DRB F1 was 0.860 with support 1,396.
For BudgetDoc Class 1 (0.5 <= F1 < 0.6), DRB recall was 0.361.
For Gemini 2.5 Flash on RVL-CDIP, mean F1 declined from 0.86 at a zero-token reasoning budget to 0.81 at 2,048 tokens, a reported 6% over-thinking penalty.

canonical_statement: The authors characterize cross-model selection as exploratory and explicitly state that DRB is not claimed to be a routing system; dedicated multi-provider routing architectures are left for future work.
Appendix GPT-effort sensitivity shows DRB F1 remains close to GPT low, medium, and high effort baselines on CDIP and CheckboxQA, while TAT-DQA is consistently lower.
Adapting DRB to new model providers or unobserved model architectures requires collecting a calibration sample of configuration-outcome pairs and fine-tuning the estimator.

The evaluation is restricted to document-centric tasks in which visual layout and structural complexity drive reasoning success; general-purpose QA, code generation, and open-ended creative tasks were not evaluated.
Hierarchical budget scanning can add operational latency, making the framework less suitable for ultra-low-latency or real-time pipelines.
Cross-family model selection exhibits a calibration mismatch and materially lower F1 than the oracle, indicating that explicit multi-provider supervision is needed for cross-provider routing.

The authors conclude that a roughly 1B-parameter multimodal estimator can provide actionable pre-flight estimates for per-sample reasoning-budget selection on document tasks, with the strongest value in high-cost reasoning settings.
The paper states that BudgetDoc and the DRB baseline are released to support research on sample-level LLM performance estimation and compute-optimal inference.
